newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish government warned on costly farm policy.
newsitem.headline: Turkish government warned on costly farm policy.

text.p: Mistakes in the Turkish government's grain production policies are costly and will persist unless it takes action, according to traders, millers and pasta producers who attended a three-day international conference here.

Last year, Turkey, a major producer of wheat and other grains, had to import wheat and sugar, two of its chief commodities, to make up for shortfalls caused by inadequate government subsidies and a failure to fight bug damage.
"The most important task in effective grain agriculture is planning and it is the responsibility of the government," said Rint Akyuz, head of Rotel foreign trade company.

"A wise agricultural policy will help the government to direct the farmer but its function should not go beyond that," he told the international grains conference in the southern Turkish city of Antalya.

Akyuz's view that the government, appointed in late June, lacked a firm farm policy was shared by many other Turkish participants at the conference, which was attended by some 200 grain traders, officials and producers from all over the world.
"The government should give subsidy prices in line with free market rules, not with political concerns," he said.

Halil Sariaslan, a consultant for the influential Union of Chambers and Trade Bourses (TOBB), said the role of the government in farm policies should be redefined since the present "populist" policies would "only work to the detriment of agriculture in the country", where half of the 65-million population makes its living from farming.
"New policies should be made to enable and promote the private sector's entry into the markets, which the government should only monitor, not manipulate," he told the conference.

The government buys grain and other industrially-used farm products like sugar beet from farmers, paying prices which can be up to 50 percent above world levels. The financing of purchases is usually met by domestic and foreign borrowing.

This year's purchase prices pleased beet and grain farmers, and the government, which imposed taxes on wheat and corn imports last weekend to encourage use of local supplies, said Turkey would not need to import wheat and sugar in the next calendar year.
But millers and pasta producers said they would still import because they said the quality of local milling and durum wheat was not satisfactory.
"Difficulties in finding standard quality wheat in Turkey makes it necessary for flour millers to carry on imports," said Ilker Tanik, secretary general of Turkish Millers' Association.
He said the flour millers would benefit from an incentive for imports which are fully used to produce items for export only.
Turkey's pasta producers also said they needed higher quality imported durum wheat and two producing companies have struck import deals to import a total of about 60,000 tonnes.

Akyuz said the government should revive a plan to set up a farm board made up of government officials and sector representatives to determine farm policies and support production inputs like energy and water for flour mills.
Sariaslan said futures markets for grains and other farm products were needed to allow producers and traders to see their future clearly in terms of volatile commodities prices.
A government plan to set up one in western Turkey for cotton trading hit bureaucratic hitches, which arose between two government institutions over control of the market.

Turkey's feed meal producers also blamed the government and called it a "disgrace" to depend on imports of meals of soybean, sunflower and cotton to produce animal feeds in spite of Turkey's capacity to be self-sufficient in such items.

Turkey expects a rise in wheat production in 1996/97 to 19 million tonnes from 15.5 million in the previous year, but Western traders and local millers say the ouput for this year is unlikely to exceed 16.5 million tonnes.
